entities.name: Callixtus III
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Callixtus III, born Alonso de Borja (later Italianized as Alfonso Borgia), ascended to the papacy on April 8, 1455, becoming the first member of the formidable House of Borgia to hold the highest office of the Catholic Church. His brief pontificate, lasting just over three years until his death in August 1458, was profoundly shaped by the recent Fall of Constantinople in 1453, which galvanized his primary objective: organizing a robust crusade against the Ottoman Empire. A distinguished canon lawyer and diplomat from Valencia, Spain, his election as a compromise candidate at the age of 77 underscored the College of Cardinals' desire for stability and a strong leader in a volatile post-Constantinople Europe.

Upon his election, Callixtus III dedicated the vast majority of papal resources and diplomatic efforts to the anti-Ottoman crusade, famously vowing to 'spend his life and all his wealth in the war for the faith.' He dispatched legates across Europe, levied taxes, and even sold papal jewels to fund military preparations. His most significant achievement was the successful defense of Belgrade in 1456, where Hungarian forces under John Hunyadi, significantly bolstered by papal funds and spiritual encouragement, decisively repelled the Ottoman siege. Beyond the crusade, Callixtus III is also notable for initiating the posthumous re-trial of Joan of Arc, which culminated in the annulment of her original condemnation in 1456, clearing her name decades after her execution. However, his papacy was also marked by pronounced nepotism, as he elevated two of his young nephews to the cardinalate, including the future Pope Alexander VI.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Callixtus III's papacy was regionally significant for his vigorous, albeit ultimately limited, crusade against the Ottoman Empire which secured the vital victory at Belgrade in 1456, and for laying the foundational power structure for the notorious Borgia family within the Vatican.
